detail: V33-ROUTER-SPEC.md written; routing gap analysis + three competencies mapped
text:
That decomposes into three separately-measurable competencies, and your own numbers say only one of them is broken. Checking what exists before I write anything:

No v3.3 spec exists — only a one-line hypothesis. Writing it, because your thesis is now derivable into a corpus rather than a principle.

Wrote `V33-ROUTER-SPEC.md`. The thing worth telling you is that your thesis splits into three competencies, and **the routing part is already your best result** — it's the two epistemic halves either side of the tool call that are broken:

| | competency | measured |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | knows it doesn't hold it → reaches | **~70% fail** (69/74% invent when the receipt is absent) |
| **I** | ingests what came back → re-emits faithfully | **~31% fail** (invents even with the receipt in the prompt) |
| **O** | forms the actual call | **6–18% fail** — BFCL 94.0 / 91.0 / 82.8, frontier band |

"Pull knowledge from outside itself" is the part that already works. Every round from v1 to v3.2 optimised evidence *content* and never trained R or I as behaviours.

The gap I didn't expect: **every corpus you've built is single-world.** v3.1 was 12% answerable, v3.2 was 92% answerable. Neither teaches the model to *tell which world it's in* — and at inference that's the only thing it has to decide. So the spec interleaves three prompt classes, including one that has never existed in your data: **partial evidence** — some receipts present, some missing, target uses what's there, names the gap, routes for the rest. That's the actual conductor case and it's in zero rows today.

Two things in there I'd hold you to:

1. **False-abstention rate** — how often it declines when the receipt *was* there. Never measured, and it's the guard against the third over-correction. Train humility hard without it and you get a conductor that never conducts, which reads as compliant and is worse than a fabricator.
2. **Run the length test first.** Your "adding so much confuses them" is still confounded with content in every round. Same rows, same content, vary only excerpt length — 2,406 vs 504 chars. One run settles it, and it changes how v3.3 itself gets assembled.

detail: explained RAG failure modes: training data imbalance
text:
Let me drop the jargon.

Imagine asking someone a question they need a filing cabinet to answer. Three separate skills:

1. **Knowing the answer isn't in their head, so they go look.** Your model fails this ~70% of the time — it makes something up instead of going to the cabinet.
2. **Reading the file correctly once it's open in front of them.** Fails ~31% — it invents things even with the paper in its hand.
3. **Physically opening the right drawer.** It's good at this. 94%.

You'd assume #3 was the hard part. It isn't — that's already near the best models money can buy. The broken parts are "know you need to look" and "read it right."

**Why the training kept failing:** every dataset you built was one-sided. The first one almost never included the answer in the question. The second one almost always did. So the model never learned to *tell which situation it's in* — it just picked up a habit, and the habit is wrong half the time.

**The fix:** mix them together. Some questions where the answer genuinely isn't there — correct response is "I don't have this, I'm going to go look." Some where it is — correct response is to quote it. And some where *half* is there — use what you have, say what's missing, go get the rest. That third kind doesn't exist anywhere in your data, and it's the one your daemon actually produces all day.

**The one trap:** if you overdo teaching it to say "I don't know," you get a model that says "I don't know" when the answer was sitting right there. That looks obedient and it's useless. So it has to be measured, not assumed.

Tell me which of those lands wrong and I'll go at it from a different angle.
